sections.markdown:
## C — Unposted speed limits, regulatory and advisory speed signs, adjusting speed to conditions, driving too slowly, what sign shapes mean, school crossing signs and speeds, railroad warning and crossing signs and the railroad stop rules
Knowledge domain: the speed limits that apply when no sign is posted, how white and orange speed signs differ, how to slow for weather, why driving too slowly is dangerous, what the octagon, triangle, rectangle, pennant, diamond, pentagon and circle shapes tell you, and how to cross a school zone or railroad crossing safely.

FACT_ID: sec11-F01 | anchor: A01
Road conditions, traffic flow and the number of crashes are used to set a road's proper speed limit, and you must obey every posted limit. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec11-F02 | anchor: A01
When no limit is posted, the speed limit is 15 mph as you approach a school crosswalk. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec11-F03 | anchor: A01
When no limit is posted, the speed limit is 25 mph in any business or residential district. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec11-F04 | anchor: A01
When no limit is posted, the speed limit is 55 mph on open highways or city freeways. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec11-F05 | anchor: A01
When no limit is posted, the speed limit is 65 mph on designated open highways. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec11-F06 | anchor: A01
When no limit is posted, the speed limit is 75 mph on rural freeways. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec11-F07 | anchor: A01
A white speed limit sign with black letters is a regulatory sign showing the highest speed you may legally drive. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec11-F08 | anchor: A01
An orange sign with black letters gives a recommended safe speed for a curve, a grade or another special condition, so slow down until you are sure you can get through safely. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec11-F09 | anchor: A01
Speed limits assume the best driving conditions, so in bad weather lower your speed to one that is reasonable. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec11-F10 | anchor: A01
On wet roads, and on roads with snow or ice, reduce your speed appropriately. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec11-F11 | anchor: A01
In bad weather, double your following distance from the vehicle ahead as well as slowing down. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec11-F12 | anchor: A01
Driving too slowly can be just as dangerous as driving too fast. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec11-F13 | anchor: A01
Whenever you are slower than the traffic around you, keep to the right lane and let faster vehicles pass. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec11-F14 | anchor: A01
Traffic signs control traffic and give drivers important information. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec11-F15 | anchor: A01
A sign's shape can tell you as much about its meaning as its color or its words. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec11-F16 | anchor: A01
In heavy rain, dust storms or fog, the shape may be the only part of a sign you can make out. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec11-F17 | anchor: A02
The octagon shape is used only for stop signs, which require a complete stop. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec11-F18 | anchor: A02
A triangle-shaped sign requires you to yield the right-of-way to cross traffic or merging traffic. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec11-F19 | anchor: A02
Rectangular regulatory signs control traffic and direct your speed and direction, such as go straight or turn left, no U-turn, no left turn and no right turn. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec11-F20 | anchor: A02
Turn, curve and winding road signs warn drivers of bends in the roadway ahead. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec11-F21 | anchor: A02
Small yellow square signs may be mounted below a curve sign to show the safe speed through the curve. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec11-F22 | anchor: A02
A pennant-shaped sign marks where a no-passing zone begins. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec11-F23 | anchor: A02
Yellow diamond-shaped signs warn of a possible danger ahead. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec11-F24 | anchor: A03
A permanent five-sided, pentagon-shaped school crossing sign warns that children may be crossing at any time of day. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec11-F25 | anchor: A03
School crossing signs may be yellow, and many Arizona school districts are posting yellow-green ones. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec11-F26 | anchor: A03
You must also obey portable signs sometimes set in the middle of the road, and from the first sign until past the school crossing sign the top speed is 15 mph. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec11-F27 | anchor: A03
When the portable school signs are not out, the area's normal speed limit applies. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec11-F28 | anchor: A03
Passing another vehicle in a school crossing zone is prohibited. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec11-F29 | anchor: A03
Follow the crossing guard's instructions and stop completely whenever anyone is in the crosswalk. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec11-F30 | anchor: A03
A circle-shaped railroad warning sign tells you a railroad crossing is ahead. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec11-F31 | anchor: A03
The railroad crossing sign marks the exact location of the crossing. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec11-F32 | anchor: A03
Stop no closer than 15 feet from the nearest rail when you see flashing red lights, a lowered barricade, ringing bells or a flagger warning of a train or other on-track equipment. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec11-F33 | anchor: A03
Do not cross the tracks until every signal has stopped and the barricade has risen all the way. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec11-F34 | anchor: A03
Never drive around or under a lowered crossing barricade. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec11-F35 | anchor: A03
Assume that a train or other rail equipment could be coming on any track, at any hour. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec11-F36 | anchor: A03
Never let yourself get trapped on a railroad crossing. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec11-F37 | anchor: A03
If your vehicle stalls on the tracks, get out of it. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0042]

Misconceptions: an orange speed sign is advice for a curve or grade, while a white sign is the legal maximum; the school-zone speed applies only while the portable signs are out, otherwise the normal limit applies; the rural freeway limit and the designated open highway limit are different numbers; driving well below the flow of traffic in the left lane is not the safe choice, slower traffic keeps right.
Mnemonics: Octagon stops, triangle yields, pennant says no passing, pentagon means school, circle means railroad ahead.
Glossary: regulatory sign means a sign that states a law you must obey; advisory speed means a recommended safe speed on an orange or small yellow sign; pennant means the sideways triangular no-passing sign; on-track equipment means rail vehicles other than trains that use the tracks.
Dynamic facts: unposted speed limits are set by statute and can be amended, and which Arizona school districts use yellow-green school signs is a local choice that keeps changing.
